paragraphs: Concept drift occurs when the relationship a predictive model is trying to learn changes over a sequence of observations. This paper addresses uncertainty about when the latest change happened. Instead of committing immediately to one change location, the method maintains a probability distribution over possible locations of the most recent drift point.

The approach trains models on blocks of consecutive observations and uses their predictions to compare candidate explanations of the data. Bayesian model comparison updates the probabilities assigned to possible drift locations. Candidates with low probability are then removed. This combines a probabilistic account of uncertainty with a pruning mechanism that reduces the number of possibilities the method continues to track.

The experiments compare this approach with a nonprobabilistic drift method and a probabilistic change-point detection method. The proposed method generally improves accuracy, speed, or both in those comparisons. The finding supports maintaining several plausible drift locations while discarding weak candidates, without claiming that every comparison improves both predictive accuracy and computational speed.
neurips-2010-a-bayesian-approach-to-conc.tldr: A Bayesian method tracks uncertainty about the latest concept drift and generally improves accuracy or speed in the reported comparisons.

paragraphs: The paper asks how a visual system can decide which orientation dominates at a particular image location. Treating this as a decision problem produces a new orientation measure resembling the one used in SIFT. The contribution connects a useful computer vision representation with a computational account of biological visual processing.

The authors show that a network following the sequence of operations in a standard model of primary visual cortex can compute the measure. They call the resulting representation bioSIFT. Its units exhibit properties associated with V1 neurons, including suppression by competing orientations, sparse responses, and independence. This connection also emphasizes the role of contrast normalization in constructing useful visual features.

To test its practical value, the authors replace the Gabor units in an HMAX network with bioSIFT units. They report significant classification gains, reaching leading performance among biologically inspired models and competing with the best nonbiological recognition systems considered. The results support both the computational usefulness of the representation and the proposed connection between SIFT-like features and biological vision.
neurips-2010-a-biologically-plausible-ne.tldr: bioSIFT connects orientation features with a plausible V1 computation and improves classification when incorporated into an HMAX network.

paragraphs: Sparse linear regression seeks a predictive coefficient vector with relatively few nonzero entries. This paper considers the additional situation in which there is prior knowledge about the pattern those entries should form. The goal is to use that structure when learning the coefficients, rather than encouraging sparsity without regard to which variables appear together.

The authors introduce a family of convex penalties that express structural knowledge through constraints on coefficient magnitudes. The family includes the familiar l1 norm while accommodating other practically and theoretically relevant sparsity patterns. They establish properties of these penalties and identify examples where the penalty can be computed explicitly, helping connect the general construction to usable regression objectives.

The paper also provides a convergent optimization algorithm for least-squares regression regularized by these penalties. Numerical simulations demonstrate benefits from exploiting structured sparsity and report advantages over Lasso and related methods. Together, the construction and algorithm provide a way to encode more informative assumptions about variable selection while retaining a convex optimization formulation.
neurips-2010-a-family-of-penalty-functio.tldr: A family of convex regression penalties incorporates prior knowledge about sparsity patterns and includes Lasso’s l1 penalty as a special case.

paragraphs: Rank aggregation combines several input orderings into a single ranking. Probabilistic approaches describe how rankings arise, but the paper identifies a tension in existing models between expressive power and computational cost. Its proposed CPS model aims to describe a broad range of ranking behavior while keeping learning and prediction manageable.

The model builds a permutation through a sequence of stages and uses a coset-permutation distance to describe ranking differences. Different permutation distances can induce this distance, giving the model flexibility. Computational efficiency comes from decomposing the permutation probability across stages and from the efficient computation of most of the associated distances. These two design choices address expressiveness and cost together.

The authors apply CPS to supervised rank aggregation and derive algorithms for learning the model and producing rankings. Experiments on public datasets show that the resulting algorithms can achieve leading ranking accuracy while being much faster than previous algorithms. The reported contribution is therefore a flexible probabilistic representation accompanied by practical learning and inference procedures.
neurips-2010-a-new-probabilistic-model-f.tldr: The CPS model combines flexible ranking distances with stagewise probabilities to support accurate and efficient supervised rank aggregation.

paragraphs: A point process describes events such as neural spikes occurring over time. Comparing only average firing rates or time-varying rates can miss differences in the underlying process, making hypothesis tests misleading. This paper develops comparison measures intended to capture the probability structure beyond those rate summaries, with applications including model fitting and detecting changes.

The proposed family of nonparametric divergences extends Kolmogorov–Smirnov and Cramér–von Mises testing ideas to point processes through stratification. A central property is that the divergence is zero exactly when the underlying point processes are the same. This makes the comparison sensitive to distinctions that rate-based descriptions alone need not capture.

The authors prove consistency and show that the measures can be estimated efficiently from observations. They also demonstrate an application in which a divergence serves as the objective for finding optimally matched spike trains. The work thus links a stronger statistical comparison of event processes to an optimization task, rather than treating the divergence only as a test statistic.
neurips-2010-a-novel-family-of-non-param.tldr: New point-process divergences compare probability structure beyond firing rates and support consistent testing and spike-train matching.

paragraphs: Some variable-selection problems require choosing predefined groups of variables, and a variable may belong to several groups. This overlap creates a computational challenge for a generalized group-lasso formulation: an existing implementation explicitly replicates variables appearing in multiple groups. The paper develops a different optimization procedure for that same regularized learning problem.

The method combines proximal updates in the original, or primal, problem with a constrained Newton method in a smaller dual problem. The reduced dual space corresponds to active groups. By organizing computation this way, the procedure handles group overlap without duplicating the data, offering a scalable alternative to implementations based on replicated variables.

The authors state that the procedure can tackle high-dimensional problems without first reducing the dimensionality of the data. Numerical simulations demonstrate computational advantages over leading algorithms that use duplication. The contribution is primarily an optimization improvement: it makes an overlapping-group sparsity model more practical while preserving the purpose of selecting variables according to the supplied group structure.
neurips-2010-a-primal-dual-algorithm-for.tldr: A primal-dual optimization method handles overlapping group sparsity without duplicating data and shows computational advantages in simulations.

paragraphs: Bayesian games model strategic situations in which players do not have complete information. The paper introduces Bayesian action-graph games, or BAGGs, as a graphical representation for these problems. The representation can express arbitrary Bayesian games, while offering compact descriptions when a game contains useful structure.

The structures it can exploit include symmetry, independence in how actions or player types affect utilities, and probabilistic independence among type distributions. These properties matter because they can reduce how much information must be represented and processed. The authors provide an algorithm for computing expected utility and identify conditions under which its running time is polynomial.

Expected-utility computation also supports finding Bayes-Nash equilibria. The paper explains how existing algorithms for complete-information normal-form games can be adapted using the new utility algorithm. Theoretical and empirical results show significant improvements over prior approaches. The key distinction is between broad representational coverage and conditional computational efficiency: BAGGs can represent any Bayesian game, but compactness and polynomial-time utility computation depend on exploitable structure and the stated conditions.
neurips-2010-bayesian-action-graph-games.tldr: Bayesian action-graph games exploit structure in incomplete-information games to improve representation, expected-utility computation, and equilibrium calculations.

paragraphs: Comparing gene expression across species requires deciding which genes correspond to one another. Those correspondences, called ortholog matches, are unknown for many genes. Fixing uncertain matches in advance can therefore complicate the search for expression patterns shared across species and patterns specific to one species.

The paper develops a method that accepts uncertain, or soft, matches as prior information and jointly infers gene matching and expression patterns. It uses a Dirichlet process mixture model with an additional latent variable representing the matching. This lets uncertainty about correspondence participate in the analysis instead of requiring a single predetermined assignment or reducing multidimensional expression measurements to binary values.

The authors provide variational methods for learning and inference, then apply the model to immune-response data from humans and mice. They report accurate identification of shared and distinct response patterns through improved gene matchings. The result illustrates the value of treating correspondence and pattern discovery as connected inference problems, allowing expression evidence to help refine the cross-species comparison.
neurips-2010-cross-species-expression-an.tldr: A mixture model jointly refines uncertain cross-species gene matches and discovers shared or species-specific expression patterns.

paragraphs: Training image classifiers usually requires substantial manual labeling, while images collected through keyword searches provide abundant but noisy labels. The paper investigates combining these resources: a small collection of carefully labeled images and a large collection of weakly labeled web photos. Its examples use only one to ten manually labeled images per class.

The authors formulate this combination as domain adaptation. The manually annotated examples define the target domain where predictions should work well, while web photos form a source domain supplying additional training information. This framing makes the objective explicit: information from the larger, noisier collection should help reduce prediction error on the target domain.

Experiments report significant recognition improvements over the best published results using the same number of strongly labeled examples, including a reported 65% improvement with five examples per class. The classifiers are also reported to be an order of magnitude faster to train and evaluate than the strongest competing method. These findings show that abundant weak supervision can be useful when incorporated through an appropriate adaptation approach.
neurips-2010-exploiting-weakly-labeled-w.tldr: Domain adaptation combines a few carefully labeled images with many noisy web images to improve recognition and computational efficiency.

paragraphs: Outliers can be unusual because of their output values, but they can also be isolated in the input space. This paper focuses on observations in sparsely populated input regions. It asks how regression and classification methods can respond more cautiously to those observations while retaining useful estimates in regions with denser evidence.

The authors construct heavy-tailed process priors from Gaussian processes using a copula. These priors can produce selective shrinkage: estimates in sparse regions are pulled back more strongly than estimates in dense regions. The theoretical analysis establishes this behavior when the marginal distributions of the process have sufficiently heavy tails, making tail behavior a substantive condition of the result.

Experiments on biological data complement the analysis. They indicate significant improvements in sparse regions while maintaining competitive results in dense regions. The contribution extends the role of heavy-tailed modeling beyond handling unusual outputs, showing how a prior over functions can address uneven input coverage. The reported gains support adapting shrinkage to where observations are scarce.
neurips-2010-heavy-tailed-process-priors.tldr: Sufficiently heavy-tailed process priors can shrink estimates more strongly in sparse input regions, improving robustness to isolated observations.

paragraphs: Unlabeled examples can contain useful information about classification when their positions trace a manifold, a lower-dimensional shape within the feature space. A learner may use that shape to help interpret the labeled examples. This paper investigates whether people make use of such information in a semi-supervised learning task.

The authors conduct experiments under varying conditions to test human use of the manifold. The central issue is how the structure of the available examples interacts with a preference for a simpler decision rule. In particular, people show a strong preference for a linear boundary aligned with a feature axis, even when manifold information is available.

The experiments show that people may be encouraged to use the manifold and overcome this preference. The finding therefore concerns both an available learning ability and the conditions under which it is expressed. It suggests that the presence of informative unlabeled structure alone does not ensure people will use it; their preference for a simple boundary can shape how they approach the classification task.
neurips-2010-humans-learn-using-manifold.tldr: People can be encouraged to use manifold structure in classification despite a strong preference for simple axis-aligned boundaries.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to recover interactions in a system with linear stochastic dynamics. Such a system can be represented by a directed graph whose connections describe which variables influence others during its evolution. The available evidence is an observed system trajectory spanning a time interval of length T.

The authors analyze an l1-regularized least-squares method for inferring this network. Their guarantees apply when the underlying network is sparse, meaning that relatively few interactions need to be recovered. A central feature of the analysis is that the performance guarantees remain uniform across sampling rates once the rate is sufficiently high.

This result supports describing the difficulty of network inference in terms of observation duration, or time complexity. Taking more closely spaced measurements and observing a system for longer are distinct aspects of data collection. By obtaining guarantees that do not deteriorate with changes among sufficiently high sampling rates, the paper gives theoretical substance to the idea that elapsed observation time is a meaningful resource for this inference problem.
neurips-2010-learning-networks-of-stocha.tldr: For sparse linear stochastic systems, l1-regularized network inference has guarantees uniform over sufficiently high sampling rates.

paragraphs: Clustering requires an objective that defines which groupings of data are preferable. This paper considers objectives expressible through submodular functions and introduces a minimum average cost criterion. It shows how the theory of intersecting submodular functions can be used to solve clustering problems with this form of objective.

The proposed algorithm does not require the number of clusters as an input. Instead, the properties of the supplied data determine that number through the clustering formulation. This makes selecting the grouping and determining how many groups to use parts of the same problem, rather than requiring a cluster count to be chosen beforehand.

The authors also study a version of the problem controlled by a real-valued parameter. They prove that all information about optimal clusterings across all parameter values can be computed in polynomial total time. This is a result about the entire parameterized problem, not merely one selected value. Computational experiments additionally evaluate the algorithm, complementing the theoretical connection between submodularity and clustering.
neurips-2010-minimum-average-cost-cluste.tldr: Minimum average cost clustering uses submodular structure to determine cluster counts and compute optimal-clustering information across all parameter values in polynomial time.

paragraphs: The paper introduces multivariate dyadic regression trees as a nonparametric method for learning regression functions in settings with many variables. Its central concern is adaptation: the method should accommodate both how many variables matter and how smoothly the response changes, without requiring those properties to be known in advance.

The trees are constructed by minimizing empirical prediction risk together with a new penalty that encourages sparsity. The authors prove that the resulting method can adapt simultaneously to unknown sparsity and smoothness. For the specified class of smooth functions, it achieves nearly optimal minimax convergence rates, meaning its statistical performance approaches the best worst-case rate available for that class.

Empirical results show simultaneous function estimation and variable selection in high dimensions. To make the approach usable on large learning problems, the authors also propose a greedy heuristic. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets demonstrate superior performance in the reported comparisons. The work combines a statistical justification for adaptive tree learning with a practical strategy for scaling its use.
neurips-2010-multivariate-dyadic-regress.tldr: Multivariate dyadic regression trees use a sparsity penalty to adapt to unknown variable relevance and function smoothness.

paragraphs: Estimating optical flow means estimating apparent motion in images, while detecting occlusions means identifying where visibility is blocked. The paper addresses these tasks jointly. This matters because motion estimation and visibility are connected: interpreting image changes requires accounting for both movement and the disappearance of image content behind other objects.

The authors show that the joint task can be formulated as a convex minimization problem under assumptions of Lambertian reflection and unchanging illumination. Convexity permits efficient algorithms to obtain a globally optimal solution to that formulation. The stated result accommodates any number of independently moving objects and any number of occlusion layers.

The guarantee is tied to the model and its assumptions: global optimality concerns the formulated optimization problem under those imaging conditions. The authors test their algorithm on benchmark datasets expanded to support evaluation of occlusion detection. The contribution is thus both a joint mathematical treatment of motion and visibility and an evaluation setup that explicitly assesses the occlusion component.
neurips-2010-occlusion-detection-and-mot.tldr: Under Lambertian reflection and static illumination, joint optical-flow and occlusion estimation admits a convex formulation with a globally optimal solution.

paragraphs: The paper studies an online learner that combines probability predictions from several binary classifiers. It has no advance knowledge of the input distribution or the classifiers’ performance. The desired behavior is to identify positives effectively while keeping the average false-positive rate below a specified threshold.

The initial objective has two asymptotic requirements: respect the false-positive constraint and match the true-positive rate of the best feasible convex combination of classifiers chosen in hindsight. The authors connect this objective to regret minimization with constraints and show that the original goal is unattainable. This establishes an obstacle to demanding both guarantees together in the stated online setting.

They therefore formulate a relaxed objective and provide a practical online combination algorithm that achieves it. With two classifiers, the algorithm becomes especially simple. The contribution pairs an impossibility result with a usable alternative, clarifying why the original benchmark must be weakened. Its guarantee belongs to the relaxed objective, so it should not be read as achieving the two original requirements unchanged.
neurips-2010-online-classification-with-.tldr: An unattainable online classification objective motivates a practical relaxation for improving true-positive rates under false-positive constraints.

paragraphs: Predicting program execution time often requires expert analysis to select useful features or construct a model. Building on a system that automatically extracts many features from sample executions, this paper focuses on learning the predictor itself. Its SPORE methodology uses sparse polynomial regression to describe program performance.

The two proposed algorithms select a small number of features from hundreds of candidates and build explicitly nonlinear models. Because the final model has a compact polynomial form, its selected features and their combinations could reveal which aspects of execution dominate runtime. The approach therefore aims to make prediction models useful for understanding program behavior as well as forecasting performance.

Evaluation on three widely used programs reports relative prediction error below 7% with a moderate number of training samples. Comparisons with leading sparse regression algorithms show advantages in both prediction accuracy and interpretability. These results support the value of designing sparse nonlinear models around execution-derived features, with the reported accuracy applying to the programs evaluated.
neurips-2010-predicting-execution-time-o.tldr: SPORE learns compact nonlinear runtime predictors from execution features, achieving relative errors below 7% on three evaluated programs.

paragraphs: Multi-view data describe the same underlying examples through several forms of observation. This paper seeks a shared latent representation that is useful for prediction across those views. Its large-margin learning framework makes predictive usefulness a central objective of learning the hidden subspace.

The model is an undirected latent-space Markov network. It assumes that the multi-view observations and response variables are conditionally independent given a set of latent variables. In practical terms, the hidden representation supplies the connection between the observations and what the model is trying to predict. The authors provide efficient procedures for inference and parameter estimation within this formulation.

Experiments use real video and web-image data to study the learned representations. The reported results demonstrate advantages from large-margin learning for discovering predictive latent structure and improving image classification, annotation, and retrieval. The contribution connects shared representation learning with prediction-oriented training, showing how multiple views can be brought together in a model whose latent space serves downstream visual tasks.
neurips-2010-predictive-subspace-learnin.tldr: A large-margin latent-space model learns shared predictive representations from multiple views and improves several visual tasks in experiments.

paragraphs: Manifold learning rests on the idea that high-dimensional observations lie near a lower-dimensional shape. This paper asks how many random observations are needed to fit such a shape with nearly optimal squared error. Its analysis assumes upper bounds on the manifold’s intrinsic dimension, volume, and curvature.

The authors show that empirical risk minimization can achieve this goal with a sample count independent of the surrounding space’s dimension. Their upper bound grows polynomially with curvature, exponentially with intrinsic dimension, and linearly with intrinsic volume. For constant error, a matching minimax lower bound establishes that these dependencies cannot generally be avoided within the studied setting.

The paper also improves a known upper bound on sample complexity for k-means, without claiming to close the entire gap to the lower bound. Building on the analysis, it gives a simple k-means algorithm and a method using convex programs to fit a piecewise-linear curve of specified length. Both have sample complexity independent of ambient dimension, separating statistical data requirements from the number of coordinates used to represent observations.
neurips-2010-sample-complexity-of-testin.tldr: Under geometric bounds, nearly optimal manifold fitting needs samples governed by intrinsic geometry rather than ambient dimension.

paragraphs: Structured prediction can require searching an enormous space of interdependent outputs. This paper proposes a cascade of ensembles built from tractable submodels, targeting problems with large state spaces and complicated dependencies. The aim is to reduce the candidate output space without performing inference in a single intractable model.

Each submodel contributes max-marginal scores, which describe its best achievable score subject to particular output choices. The ensemble adds and thresholds these scores to filter candidates, without requiring the submodels to agree. At each cascade level, all model parameters are learned jointly using a convex loss. Computation increases only linearly relative to learning or inference in one tractable submodel.

The authors provide a generalization bound for filtering loss, giving theoretical support specifically for the ensemble’s filtering behavior. Tests on synthetic data and articulated human pose estimation from challenging videos show significant improvements over loopy belief propagation and a leading pose model, respectively. The results support using several manageable models to narrow the search in difficult structured prediction tasks.
neurips-2010-sidestepping-intractable-in.tldr: Structured ensemble cascades combine tractable models to filter large output spaces efficiently, with theoretical and empirical support.

paragraphs: The paper develops a way to represent large collections of categorical data as points in Euclidean space using co-occurrence statistics. Its motivating application is unsupervised part-of-speech induction, where useful grammatical groupings must be discovered without supplied tags. The learned representation is intended to make those groupings accessible through clustering.

The authors start from the CODE embedding model and require every embedded point to lie on a high-dimensional unit sphere. This geometric constraint allows efficient optimization even when both the dataset and embedding dimension are large. After learning the representation, they apply k-means to the embedded data to produce the resulting groups.

The approach efficiently achieves leading results on the motivating application. The authors also analyze why the sphere constraint helps in this setting and conjecture that similar reasons could apply to other large-scale tasks. The demonstrated result concerns part-of-speech induction; the broader applicability remains a conjecture. The paper illustrates how a simple geometric restriction can improve the computational usefulness of a learned representation.
neurips-2010-sphere-embedding-an-applica.tldr: Constraining co-occurrence embeddings to a unit sphere enables efficient optimization and strong unsupervised part-of-speech induction.

paragraphs: Spike timing-dependent plasticity links changes in synaptic strength to neural activity timing. With complex spike sequences, the contributions of presynaptic and postsynaptic activity can themselves be weakened or enhanced. The paper models these changing contributions using a small system of differential equations with biophysically interpretable parameters.

The model reproduces a wide range of experimental findings and provides a way to study plasticity as a nonlinear filter of activity over time. For small periodic changes in firing rates, the authors can solve the model and examine its predictions. Synchronous rate changes produce strengthening, while at low baseline firing rates the strongest modifications occur in the theta frequency range.

The model also emphasizes low baseline spike rates and suppresses high ones. The latter finding suggests a possible mechanism for regulating network activity within plasticity itself. More broadly, the formulation provides a framework for studying interactions between neural activity and changing plasticity contributions in both spike-based and rate-based networks, connecting local synaptic dynamics with network-level modeling.
neurips-2010-spike-timing-dependent-plas.tldr: A compact dynamical model treats synaptic plasticity as a nonlinear activity filter and predicts frequency- and baseline-dependent changes.

paragraphs: The paper extends logistic regression using t-exponential families originating in statistical physics. This changes the learning objective into regularized risk minimization with a nonconvex loss. The motivation is to obtain a classifier whose loss makes learning more tolerant of incorrect training labels.

The authors derive an efficient block coordinate descent procedure for estimating the parameters. This approach optimizes blocks of parameters in turn. Although the loss is nonconvex, the paper reports that the algorithm is fairly robust to its starting values, a practical property that matters when different initializations could otherwise affect the fitted solution.

Experiments on synthetic and real datasets support both tolerance to label noise and relative robustness to initialization. These are empirical observations, rather than a claim that every initialization reaches a global optimum. The contribution combines a different statistical family, a workable optimization scheme, and evidence that the resulting classifier can handle noisy labels without being excessively sensitive to how parameter estimation begins.
neurips-2010-t-logistic-regression-934d7.tldr: t-logistic regression uses a nonconvex loss and efficient block updates, showing tolerance to label noise and relative robustness to initialization.

paragraphs: Optimal control requires reasoning about both uncertain outcomes and their value. In practical problems, probability distributions usually must be approximated, and more accurate representations can cost more to compute. This paper asks how a system should balance the decision benefits of a better approximation against the resources required to maintain it.

The authors propose a variational framework and apply it to how a population of neurons should represent a distribution under resource constraints. Their central conjecture is that population codes are organized to maximize a lower bound on the logarithm of expected utility. This makes the usefulness of a representation for valued outcomes part of the objective governing its organization.

The theory can account for a range of experimental observations, including changes in sensory receptive fields associated with reward. Its significance is to connect neural representation with both computational cost and behavioral value. The organizing principle is presented as a conjecture supported by its explanatory reach, rather than as an established universal rule for neural coding.
neurips-2010-the-neural-costs-of-optimal.tldr: A variational theory proposes that resource-limited neural representations balance computational cost against expected utility.

paragraphs: This paper asks how much training data large-margin classification needs when it uses L2 regularization. The focus is distribution-specific sample complexity: how the required number of examples depends on the distribution supplying the data. A useful answer must capture the aspects of that distribution that actually govern the learning problem.

The authors introduce the gamma-adapted dimension, a quantity calculated from the spectrum of the distribution’s covariance matrix. It summarizes distributional geometry in a form relevant to the margin. They prove both upper and lower sample-complexity bounds controlled by this quantity, connecting an achievable data requirement with a corresponding limit on what learning can accomplish.

The matching characterization establishes that gamma-adapted dimension captures the true sample complexity within the studied setting. The bounds apply to a rich family of sub-Gaussian distributions, which is the stated scope of the result. The contribution is a distribution-sensitive account of data requirements, showing how covariance structure can explain learning difficulty more precisely than a description that ignores the source distribution.
neurips-2010-tight-sample-complexity-of-.tldr: Gamma-adapted dimension tightly characterizes large-margin sample complexity for a rich family of sub-Gaussian data distributions.
